newsitem.title: GERMANY: German minister seeks foreign train investment.
newsitem.headline: German minister seeks foreign train investment.

text.p: The German government on Sunday proposed inviting foreign investment to prevent the futuristic Transrapid high-speed train project from collapsing for want of sufficient financing.

The high-speed train, propelled at over 400 km (250 miles) per hour by magnetic-levitation technology, has become a symbol of German industrial innovation on the threshhold of the 21st century and its collapse would be an embarrassment for the government.

Facing an impending financing crisis for the first Transrapid route connecting Germany's two largest cities, Berlin and Hamburg, government and industry representatives have been scrambling to find a way to save the project.

"I presume that industry is now going to muster all of its strength to operate this project with creativity and commitment," Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann told the weekly Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
"In my opinion it would also be conceivable to bring companies from other European countries on board as investors in the operating consortium and thereby reduce economic risks."
The government is financing with nearly six billion marks ($3.6 billion) the construction of the Transrapid track, but the industry consortium is responsible for the operational costs.
The consortium includes Thyssen AG and Siemens AG, Bilfinger & Berger, Hochtief and construction group Philip Holzmann.

The future of the project has been thrown into doubt because of new calculations of traffic volume and building expenses that could drive costs so high as to make the train unfeasible compared to alternatives, such as the ICE Express.
Opposition politicians, who have long preferred the ICE to building new railway infrastructure, said Wissmann's suggestion was in itself an admission that the Transrapid had no future.

"Wissmann's desperate search for new investors in the Transrapid shows that he has finally understood that German industry does not have a red cent for the Transrapid," said Gila Altmann of the environmentalist Greens party.
Berlin Social Democrat (SPD) Wolfgang Behrendt urged the government to propose an alternative route for the Transrapid that would be shorter and less costly.
Unlike the Hamburg-Berlin route, it should also be one that does not already have alternative ICE track that could be used at much less expense, he argued.
Eckhard Rohkamm, chairman of Thyssen Industrie AG, after a meeting of the Transrapid consortium last week, said he was confident that the train could be built and operated economically.
The government has ruled out raising its funding for the project and Wissmann said that although he was a strong advocate he would not support the Transrapid "at any price". ($1=1.6383 Mark)
